Reading the Ashwood Charter as an argument, not a record

Crafted fixture text, written for this test.

The temptation with a charter is to read it as a description of how a place worked. It is
better read as an attempt to settle something that was not settled. Each clause is doing
work against an opposing position that the document never states, and the shape of the
missing position can usually be recovered from how hard the clause pushes.

The signatory list pushes hardest. Fourteen names in a fixed order, in a document that
otherwise spends its care on days and fines, is a lot of effort spent on precedence. The
plain reading is that precedence was in dispute and that the drafter was on the miller's
side.

The bridge clause pushes in the opposite direction. It begins by giving the bridge to
nobody, which reads as a concession, and ends by taxing everybody who crosses it, which
reads as the actual proposal. Charters are frequently generous in their first sentence and
specific in their second.

The penalties are the least argued part of the document and, for that reason, the most
revealing. Nobody bothered to reconcile shillings with labour days because nobody expected
the two kinds of offence to be compared. The marginal dispute about conversion is a later
reader discovering the gap and being annoyed by it.
